column5: bowing to images and serving them
column6: The commentary's object-first iyyāka excludes every alternate object of worship. This command joins the two forbidden acts in one verse: bowing to carved images and serving them.

column5: YHWH or Baal; stop wavering
column6: The commentary treats exclusive worship as a decisive separation from competing masters. Elijah forces the same choice before Israel: if YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him.

column5: fearing YHWH while serving other gods
column6: The commentary insists that a single confession cannot leave competing objects in place. This verse names the divided arrangement directly: the people fear YHWH while continuing to serve their own gods.

column5: God's glory given to no other
column6: The commentary understands “you alone” as a refusal to transfer divine honor elsewhere. YHWH's self-declaration likewise withholds his glory from another and his praise from images.

column5: no savior besides YHWH
column6: The commentary says that help finally comes from the one addressed in worship. This verse makes the exclusion explicit in saving language: apart from YHWH there is no savior.

column5: turn to me and be saved; no other God
column6: The commentary's direct address makes the worshipper turn to the sole source of aid. Isaiah summons the ends of the earth to turn to God and be saved because he is God and there is no other.

column5: created by God and called his
column6: The commentary grounds belonging to God in creation before it becomes a spoken act of worship. This direct divine address joins creation, redemption, naming, and possession: “you are mine.”

column5: all gifts come from God first
column6: The commentary says the worshipper seeks help from God while God needs no supporting power. David's corporate prayer admits that people can offer only what already comes from God: “from your own hand we have given you.”

column5: God does not need creatures' offerings
column6: The commentary denies that God has the weakness or need for a helper. In a sacrifice-focused speech, God says that even if he were hungry he would not tell the worshipper, because the world and all within it are his.

column5: God's own arm brings salvation
column6: The commentary distinguishes the worshipper who asks help from the God who does not require it. This verse says that when God found no helper, his own arm brought salvation and his own wrath sustained him.

column5: arm of flesh versus God who helps
column6: The commentary allows human means but refuses to make them the final ground of aid. Hezekiah contrasts the enemy's “arm of flesh” with YHWH, who is with Judah to help it and fight its battles.

column5: God supports the hand of one who falls
column6: The commentary's traveler image includes help that keeps a person from collapsing under the way's burden. This verse says that though the faithful person falls, YHWH upholds that person's hand.

column5: God's hand leads and holds the traveler
column6: The commentary connects help with guidance on the way. The psalmist says that even at the farthest place God's hand will lead and his right hand will hold him fast.

column5: God guides the redeemed people to his dwelling
column6: The commentary makes the plural worshipper a community whose help opens toward a journey and destination. The song after the sea says that God's steadfast love led the people he redeemed and guided them toward his holy habitation.

column5: teach your way; unite my heart to fear your name
column6: The commentary joins a single object of worship to the road imagery and to a heart not divided among masters. This prayer asks God to teach his way and to make the speaker's heart one in fearing God's name.

column5: worship God in spirit and truth
column6: The commentary extends worship beyond a narrow set of ritual acts into a whole posture of submission. Jesus' saying defines fitting worship by its relation to God's Spirit and truth rather than to an external location or rite.

column5: bowing before Jesus and saying “Lord, help me”
column6: The commentary directs both worship and the explicit request for help to Allah alone. In this healing scene, the woman bows before Jesus and addresses to him the direct plea, “Lord, help me,” forming a particularly close Christian counter-narrative.

column5: one God, the Father; one Lord, Jesus Christ
column6: The commentary's exclusive divine address has one undivided addressee. Paul preserves “one God, the Father” while placing “one Lord, Jesus Christ” within the same creational confession, a distinctively Christian reconfiguration of exclusive devotion.

column5: every knee bends at Jesus' name
column6: The commentary treats bodily submission in worship as due only to God. This eschatological Christian scene says that every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bend at Jesus' name.

column5: every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord
column6: The commentary's direct confession separates the one worshipped from all rivals. This verse gives universal confession of Jesus Christ as Lord while directing the resulting glory to God the Father, a two-term Christian formulation absent from the commentary's formula.

column5: shared heavenly praise of God and the Lamb
column6: The commentary's heavenly worship returns praise away from creatures to God alone. Revelation's universal hymn offers blessing, honor, glory, and might together to the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb, an explicit alternative heavenly distribution of praise.

column5: asking the Father in Jesus' name
column6: The commentary makes direct petition itself part of exclusive worship. Jesus instructs disciples to ask the Father in his name, providing a Christian pattern of petition mediated through Jesus.

column5: one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus
column6: The commentary's worshipper addresses God without a named mediating figure. This confession likewise says “one God” but adds one mediator between God and humanity, the human Christ Jesus.

column5: the Spirit helps weakness in prayer
column6: The commentary makes asking for help an act inside worship and acknowledges that the burden exceeds the worshipper's strength. Paul says the Spirit helps human weakness precisely where people do not know how to pray as they ought.

column5: Jesus asks the Father to keep disciples from the evil one
column6: The commentary links belonging and reliance on God to protection from Satan's authority. Jesus' prayer asks the Father not to remove the disciples from the world but to keep them from the evil one.

column5: grace sufficient in weakness
column6: The commentary presents help as what enables a servant to stand under a task rather than as an escape from all burden. The divine reply to Paul calls grace sufficient and power perfected in weakness.

column5: make every request known to God
column6: The commentary leaves the object of aid in 1:5 deliberately open to every need while fixing its addressee. Paul likewise tells believers to bring requests about everything to God by prayer, petition, and thanksgiving.

column5: God restores, confirms, strengthens, establishes
column6: The commentary's help supports endurance beneath worship's weight and protects the devoted. This promise says that after suffering, the God of all grace will restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish the believers.

column5: in life and death, we belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary stretches worship beyond a momentary rite into a declaration of who owns one's whole life. Paul says that whether believers live or die, they are the Lord's.

column5: bought at a price; glorify God in the body
column6: The commentary makes belonging to God encompass more than a discrete ritual act. This verse joins being bought at a price to the command to glorify God in the body.

column5: offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe
column6: The commentary glosses worship as humility carried to its limit. Hebrews calls the community to offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe in response to the kingdom it receives.

column5: servants worship day and night and are sheltered
column6: The commentary's “we” is a protected community whose worship is ongoing. Revelation pictures the multitude before God's throne serving him day and night, while the enthroned one shelters them.

column5: the church prays earnestly to God for Peter
column6: The commentary uses a plural voice for direct aid-seeking within a community. During Peter's imprisonment, the church's response is persistent prayer to God on his behalf.

column5: the Lord stands by and strengthens the servant
column6: The commentary's avn is support that stands behind a burdened person. Paul reports that the Lord stood by him and strengthened him for the proclamation entrusted to him.

column5: acknowledge God in all ways; paths made straight
column6: The commentary lets 1:5's help-seeking reach forward to the straight path while keeping God before the worshipper's own action. Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one's ways results in God making one's paths straight.

column5: send wisdom to labor alongside the petitioner
column6: The commentary says aid can be an enabling companion while its ultimate source remains God. Solomon's prayer asks God to send Wisdom from the holy heavens so that she may be with him and labor with him.

column5: make God's will one's own will
column6: The commentary explains worship as obedient belonging, not a merely timed ceremony. This rabbinic maxim tells the disciple to make God's will like one's own will and to set aside one's own will before God's.
